newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France dismisses EMU budget pressure speculation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France dismisses EMU budget pressure speculation.

text.p: The French government on Thursday dismissed mounting media speculation about its ability to reduce the public deficit enough to pass the fitness test for joining a single euro currency, and vowed to do all that was necessary.

In the warm-up for a May parliamentary debate on what is set to be another thrifty budget for 1998, the press is questioning whether the government will have to do more than planned to get the deficit down to three percent of national wealth this year.

But, despite several "worst scenario" reports suggesting the deficit would overshoot the three percent mark needed to qualify for European monetary union (EMU), government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said there was no reason to worry.

Government and social security spending had been brought under control and healthy economic growth should ensure enough revenues to balance the equation, he said. In any case, further steps would be taken if there was any slippage.
"We have no budget problems at this stage, we're mastering spending like has never been done," Lamassoure told RTL radio. "Social security spending has also been reined in like never before.
"If we were to note during the year that revenues were not coming in fast enough, then we would have to take additional measures. But we already have a margin of manoeuvre," he said.
The government has already decided to freeze a further 10 billion in spending credits for this year since unveiling its initial 1997 budget plans.

Nevertheless, several newspapers have been highlighting the risks of weaker-then-expected tax receipts and shortfalls in other revenues making it hard to cut the social security deficit to the 30 billion francs ($5.2 billion) the government is counting on.

French daily Le Monde added to the turmoil after Lamassoure spoke on Thursday, saying the budget arm of the finance ministry had produced a confidential "forecast note" which said the 1997 public deficit could hit 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) taking account of the cutback measures so far planned.
The newspaper, which is issued in the afternoon, said it had been refused a copy of the note by the finance ministry but that "very good sources" had confirmed the figures.

It highlighted, however, that the finance ministry division had the task of enumerating all the possible risks of overshoot and that there was also a scenario which saw the 1997 deficit at 3.3 percent of GDP if there was firm growth and better revenues.
Part of the "worst scenario" calculation for this year was a social security deficit of 47 billion francs, 17 billion more than planned.
In a similar vein, 1998's deficit could hit 4.5 percent, or four percent including corrective steps, again including a hefty social security deficit of 58 billion francs, the paper said.
Lamassoure, who also has budget responsibilities, said that growth this year should secure the revenues needed after a poor flow of income in 1996 due to slower GDP growth.
"This year the pace of economic growth is rising rapidly, we're at a pace of between two and three percent and revenues will thus start coming in again," he said.
"If it turned out that there were any reasons to prompt us to make further savings, we would go further. Last year we froze 20 billion (extra spending credits), we can go further this year," he said.
French GDP growth was 1.3 percent in 1996 and the government is forecasting a minimum of 2.3 percent economic growth in 1997.
Economists believe the question of getting a public deficit of three percent of GDP this year is above all one of political will and that the government will do what is needed to produce this figure.

The parliament is due to discuss the 1998 budget in mid-May. After using a transer of 37.5 billion francs from France Telecom in its 1997 budget and deficit calculations, the pressure is on to find similar resources to cut the deficit further next year.

Le Monde highlighted that some people have suggested that the government may seek to tap funds from the 60 billion in equity funds of the Caisses d'Epargne savings bank group. ($ = 5.810 French Francs)
